question: ‘Money is coined liberty,’ wrote Russian author Fyodor Dostoyevsky in the 19th century about his time in prison. He was referring to cash, as modern means of payment did not exist at the time. In the 21st century, however, supranational organisations are increasingly pushing digital means of payment on to us in order to take control over all payment flows and make citizens entirely transparent vessels.

On 22 August 2025, for example, the Financial Times reported that the EU wished to fasttrack the development of the digital euro. Brussels is now even looking into the possibility of operating the digital euro on a public blockchain such as Ethereum or Solana. This move would be highly controversial, as blockchain technology functions like a decentralised digital public logbook.

Every transaction is stored, cannot be altered retrospectively and can be viewed by every user. Although the information is encrypted, each wallet has a unique address. Anyone who knows this address can track all of a person's transactions – effectively putting an end to financial privacy and constituting a massive encroachment on fundamental civil liberties.1 1.
Is the Commission planning to accelerate the introduction of the digital euro, and if so, for when?
Can the Commission rule out the possibility that the digital euro will be operated on a public blockchain, where every wallet transaction would potentially be traceable?
What specific measures is the Commission taking to fully protect citizens’ financial privacy, or is it planning to abolish it altogether?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2025) Following discussions in the Eurogroup, where Member States expressed their wish to reach an agreement on the proposed Regulation on the digital euro1 in a timely manner, the Danish Presidency has stated its intention to seek a general approach in the Council. The Commission is supportive of this goal.

The proposed Regulation is technology-neutral and hence does not prescribe any specific technical solutions for the digital euro infrastructure. Within the framework of the Regulation, which defines the essential elements of the digital euro, the European Central Bank (ECB) is responsible for decisions on technological aspects and implementation.

The ECB has recently published the outcome of its public procurement procedures for subcontractors, whose input will inform its decision-making process. Safeguarding the privacy of digital euro users remains of paramount importance. The Commission and the ECB have repeatedly underlined that the digital euro aims to provide stronger privacy protection than existing private payment instruments.

In particular, the offline payments will ensure cash-like privacy, meaning that only the two parties involved in a transaction will have knowledge of it and its details, and for the online payments, when the ECB settles these payments, it will not know the identity of the users involved. The proposed Regulation sets out strict rules governing the use of personal data by payment service providers and the ECB.

It explicitly stipulates that the ECB will have no access to data that can identify the individual, while payment service providers will be permitted to access personal information necessary for customer due diligence, anti-money-laundering measures, and fraud prevention.
1 COM/2023/369 final, herein referred to as the proposed Regulation.
